title: How do you create brainstorming buckets quickly when your mind goes blank?
description: Simple splits for brainstorming for case interviews. When you need buckets fast for "What else could they do?" A checklist, a worked example and how to say…
hook: When your mind goes blank, pick a simple pair, such as internal versus external, revenue versus costs or short term versus long term, and use the two halves as your buckets. Better still, split the number you are explaining into its parts, because a split that can be measured tells you where to look next.
body:
When it helps

Use a simple split when you need buckets fast for "What else could they do?" or "What could explain this?" It is the emergency version of the method in the brainstorming guide: it keeps your answer organised even when no tailored structure comes to mind.

The splits

  • Internal vs external
  • Short term vs long term
  • Revenue vs costs
  • Supply vs demand
  • Existing vs new customers
  • Organic vs inorganic (build vs buy)
  • Financial vs non-financial
  • Quantitative vs qualitative

Each pair is MECE by design: everything falls on one side or the other, and nothing falls on both.

An example: museum visitors

"How could a museum increase visitor numbers?" Pick a split: internal versus external. Internal: new exhibitions, longer opening hours on summer evenings, a better café, easier online booking. External: partnerships with schools, tourism boards and hotels, and events with the city. In ten seconds you have two clean buckets, and you sound organised even with no time to prepare.

Prefer splits you can measure

Generic pairs organise ideas. Splitting the number itself also finds the problem. Suppose a bike-sharing service asks why its revenue fell. Start with revenue = rides × revenue per ride. If rides are down, split rides by time, place or customer. If revenue per ride is down, look at fares, ride length, discounts and user mix.

In illustrative numbers: the service used to have 100,000 rides a week, 60,000 on weekdays and 40,000 at weekends. Weekend rides are unchanged, but weekday rides fell 20% to 48,000. Total rides are now 88,000, down 12%.

The whole fall is in weekday riding, which points to commuters. Now look at office attendance, bikes available at busy stations in the morning, and any weekday price change. One measurable split narrowed the problem more than any list of ideas could.

Other useful cuts: time (weekday or weekend), place (central or suburban), customer (commuters or tourists) and channel (app or partner). Choose the cut most likely to explain the problem, not all four.

How it sounds in an interview

"Let me split this into what the client can change itself and what involves outside partners. On the internal side, I'd look at..."

Or, for a number:

"Revenue is rides times revenue per ride. Could I see which of the two has fallen, and whether it's weekdays or weekends?"

Common mistakes

  • Picking a split that does not fit, such as short term versus long term for a question about causes.
  • Using one generic pair for every case. Interviewers notice.
  • Stopping at the buckets. A split is only useful with specific ideas underneath and a priority at the end.

Practise it

1. A bakery's profit fell. Which simple split do you use first, and what is your next question?

Show the answer

Revenue versus costs, because profit is revenue minus costs. Next question: "Has revenue fallen, have costs risen, or both?" Then split the side that moved, for example revenue into customers × spend per visit.

2. A charity wants to raise more money. Give two buckets and two ideas in each.

Show the answer

Existing donors versus new donors. Existing: move one-off donors to monthly giving; ask for gifts in wills. New: corporate partnerships; events that bring in younger supporters. Start with monthly giving, as keeping a donor is usually cheaper than finding a new one.

Where to practise next

Build speed with the structuring drills and the quick structuring prompts, then use a measurable split in a full case such as Harborline Ferries.
